name: League of Women Voters Education Fund (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US's people, whose government the work defends and reforms (the redistricting branch's people are in the US states that adopted commissions); the spillover abroad (a side-effect share of the US value) isn't assigned to countries.
summary: The League of Women Voters Education Fund, the 501(c)(3) of the League of Women Voters (the League of Women Voters of the United States is a 501(c)(4), and gifts to it aren't tax-deductible, so this models the Education Fund only), spent $11.3 million of its own money in the year to June 2025, beside $5.4 million of donated legal services and advertising that count as the donors' resources, on VOTE411.org, voter registration, voting-rights litigation and reform campaigns. Four branches: its direct work's share of the US pro-democracy field's yearly cut in the chance that the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030 (about 32% of the result); its voter information and registration, 73% of its spending, credited in the same cut at the shared weight for turnout and civic-education dollars (about 32%), with a side effect for what it changes in who is elected, judged a tenth of an access reform's effect per dollar (about 10%); its 1% share of the movement that moved 79 million Americans' maps to redistricting commissions since 2008 (about 11%); and its other reforms (voting access, the Electoral College, DC statehood), judged a quarter as effective per dollar as the redistricting movement (about 14%). With its next dollar at 52.5% of the average, it comes to about 0.012 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars; the result turns most on the years a win counts, the field's effect on the risk (both judgments), the income gain of democracy and the next-dollar figure, and all four branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: The Education Fund's own spending in the year to 30 June 2025 on its seven programme columns, with its management and fundraising, from its audited statements, less the donated legal services and advertising recorded in them (Convention 2). The League of Women Voters of the United States, the 501(c)(4), is left out: gifts to it aren't tax-deductible. The programme is split four ways for the branches: direct work against a slide, redistricting reform, other reforms, and voter information.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Who the work reaches: everyone governed by US democracy (the slide and voter-information branches), and the people in the states that moved their maps to commissions since 2008 (the redistricting branch). VOTE411's 7.6 million users and the 482,000 voters registered (the annual report) aren't counted per person or per vote: voter information counts through what it changes (the family's rule).

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the work changes: the chance that US democracy slides to a hybrid regime, valued by the income a slide would cost as it builds up; and reforms within the democracy (fair maps first, then voting access and the rest), valued as a share of democracy's income gain. Each counts the whole field's or movement's effect; the Education Fund's share is in the adjustments.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's own discounts for trust in the estimate, the Education Fund's share of its field's resources, delivery and missing data; the canonical rows are their averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled programmes, including overhead
rows.explainer: The Education Fund's whole own spending in the year: what a year of its work costs.

rows.label: Share of the programme acting on a democratic slide directly
rows.explainer: Work as direct as the field's 'direct' dollar (@democracy.field_direct_share: litigation, election protection, checks on executive power): the national litigation team and its voter-protection work (the annual report counts 11.2 million voters protected through litigation, among them the suit that blocked the 2025 executive order requiring documentary proof of citizenship and the North Carolina Supreme Court certification case; its redistricting suits, 12 of 59 federal cases, count here, not in the redistricting branch, whose wins and resources leave litigation out), the April 2025 lobbying of every congressional office to enforce checks and balances, and the legal-action prong of Women Defend Democracy and Unite and Rise 8.5. Anchor: the Advocacy column without its donated legal work is $0.73 million, 8.8% of the programme, and part of it is lobbying for reforms; parts of Mission impact and Communications serve the litigation and rapid response. Judged 15% (8% to 30%), under Common Cause Education Fund's 35% because the League runs no Election Protection hotline of that size and its lawsuits are mostly argued by donated counsel, whose work isn't its spending.

rows.label: Share of the programme spent on redistricting reform
rows.explainer: People Powered Fair Maps, the League's campaign for citizens' redistricting commissions, run mostly by state Leagues: the reference class is national support for state Leagues' commission campaigns with no national column of its own. In this year that was Ohio's 2024 Issue 1 (LWV Ohio in the coalition; lost, November 2024); state Leagues were also in the coalitions behind California's, Michigan's, Colorado's, Utah's and Virginia's commissions. The accounts have no redistricting column and the year's annual report names no national commission campaign; the redistricting work it does show is litigation (12 of 59 federal cases, p. 15), which counts in bs_direct_share, since the movement's wins and resources leave fair-maps litigation out. Judged 2% (1% to 6%), below Common Cause Education Fund's national redistricting column (3.7% of its programme), since this Education Fund has no such team and the state Leagues' own spending isn't its.

rows.label: Share of the programme on other reforms (voting access, the Electoral College, DC statehood, money in politics, courts)
rows.explainer: Reform work within the democracy: lobbying and action alerts for federal voting-rights and access bills (185,573 letters and faxes to Congress in the year), the One Person One Vote campaign to abolish the Electoral College (launched spring 2024), DC statehood, money-in-politics rules and the 2025 study of the federal judiciary. Most of the rest of the Advocacy column and a part of Communications. Judged 10% (5% to 20%).

rows.label: Share of the programme on voter information, registration and turnout
rows.explainer: The rest, about 73%: VOTE411.org (7.6 million users in the year, 55,000 candidates profiled), voter registration (482,000 registered, 176 grants to Leagues), 21 million voter contacts, candidate forums and debates, and the communications, partnerships, member services and meetings behind them. Not reform work: it counts in the voter-information branch only.

rows.explainer: Everyone in the US: the slide branch's people; the redistricting and other-reform branches' people are among them.

rows.label: People released, cleared or kept out of detention by casework in the year
rows.explainer: The Education Fund does no casework that frees people: the template's casework branch stays at 0.

rows.label: Long-run income gain from staying a democracy (share of GDP per person)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): Acemoglu et al. (2019)'s long-run income effect of democracy, read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain a slide to a hybrid regime would lose
rows.explainer: The shared figure: a slide to a hybrid regime loses part of democracy's gain, not all of it.

rows.label: Long-run income loss of a slide per person per year, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: The income a slide would cost each person each year once it had built up, on the site's log scale.

rows.label: Chance the US falls to a hybrid regime before 2030
rows.explainer: The shared forecast (facts/democracy.json), the stake for every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Relative cut in that chance from one year of the whole US pro-democracy field's work
rows.explainer: The shared figure for the whole field's yearly effect; the Education Fund's share of the field is in the adjustments.

rows.label: Chance a year of the field's work averts a slide
rows.explainer: The chance removed, counted at its expected value as every model of the field does (the field's work is thousands of cases and campaigns, not one bet).

rows.label: Years from the work until a slide it averts would have come
rows.explainer: The same work year as the Common Cause Education Fund and Brennan Center models (the year to June 2025), so the same figure: the slide-date window (the Economist's reports before 2030; those for 2024 and 2025 showed no slide, so 2026 to 2028, on average 2027) measured from mid-2025, 2.5 years (1.5 to 4.5).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (slide branch)
rows.explainer: The wait until the slide would have come, at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Years over which democracy's income effect builds up
rows.explainer: The shared build-up (facts/democracy.json): a slide's loss and a reform's gain both build up over about 25 years.

rows.label: Rate for the slide's loss: the shared discount rate plus the reversal hazard
rows.explainer: A slide, once it happens, may be undone (the shared reversal rate), so the loss averted counts at the discount rate plus that hazard.

rows.label: Discounted years of the full loss averted by putting a slide off
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + bs_rate) * ln(1 + bs_rate) * ramp_years) * bs_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp of the family's 'Democracy and governance' section: a slide put off by the years counted moves its whole build-up, worth this many full-loss years after the wait.

rows.label: Income loss averted by a year of the field's work, units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Everyone in the US × the loss per person-year × the chance a year of the field removes × the discounted years, valued at the shared value of a doubled income.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that an independent redistricting commission brings
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): share of democracy's income gain that an independent redistricting commission brings.

rows.label: Income gained per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption) (redistricting branch)
rows.explainer: The reform's share of democracy's long-run income gain, per person-year, on the log scale.

rows.label: Years from a year's work until a commission's first maps are used
rows.explainer: As in the Common Cause Education Fund model: a campaign takes about a year to win, and a commission first draws after the next census: California 2008 → 2011 maps, Michigan and Colorado 2018 → 2021, Virginia 2020 → 2021, Ohio 2015 → 2021. Judged 4 years (2 to 8).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (redistricting branch)
rows.explainer: The wait until the first commission maps, at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Discount rate plus repeal hazard (redistricting branch)
rows.explainer: Won reforms of how elections work are often undone (the shared repeal rate): Missouri's 2018 reform was repealed in 2020, Utah's legislature reversed much of Proposition 4, and California's 2025 Proposition 50 set the commission's congressional map aside until 2030.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years a won commission counts (its ramp brought forward)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + maps_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + maps_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + maps_rate) * ln(1 + maps_rate) * ramp_years) * maps_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp: the reform brought forward by the years counted moves its whole build-up, at the discount rate plus the repeal hazard, after the wait.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the redistricting movement's work (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People newly under a commission per year × the gain per person-year × the discounted years, valued at the shared value of a doubled income.

rows.label: A dollar of the other reform work against a dollar of the redistricting movement
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json): a dollar of other reform work (voting access, money in politics, ethics, media) against a dollar of the redistricting movement.

rows.label: Units of value per year of reform work the size of the redistricting movement, other reforms (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The redistricting movement's yearly value scaled by the other reforms' relative effect: the Education Fund's share is its spending on them over that movement's resources (oth_attribution_share).

rows.label: Income loss averted by a year of the field's work, voter-information branch (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Voter information counts through what it changes: like the field's other turnout drives and civic education, it acts on the chance of a slide less directly than litigation does. The field's yearly cut (bs_field_cut) is the whole field's, turnout drives included, and the field's resources weight such dollars at @democracy.field_indirect_relative_effect (bs_field_spending); this branch credits the Education Fund's voter-information dollars at that same weight (vi_attribution_share). Its effect on who is elected outside a slide is a side effect below.

rows.label: Years a won reform or postponed slide counts
rows.explainer: The shared number of years a won reform (or a slide put off) counts before it would have come anyway (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Whole field's resources as a multiple of its institutional philanthropy
rows.explainer: The shared figure: 501(c)(4) money, individual donors and pro bono work on top of foundations' grants.

rows.label: Share of the field doing direct work against a slide
rows.explainer: The shared figure: litigation, election protection, checks on power and election-official support, against the rest of the field.

rows.label: Effect of an indirect dollar on a slide, relative to a direct dollar
rows.explainer: The shared figure, weighting the field's indirect dollars in its resources.

rows.label: The pro-democracy field's resources in the year, in direct-work dollars of 2025
rows.explainer: As in the Brennan Center, Protect Democracy and Common Cause Education Fund models: institutional philanthropy × the whole field's multiple, weighted by each dollar's effect on a slide, in 2025 prices.

rows.label: The Education Fund's share of the field's resources against a slide (direct work)
rows.explainer: Its direct work's own spending over the field's resources in direct-work dollars (Convention 2). Its voter-information dollars count in their own branch at the indirect weight, and its reform dollars only in the reform branches, as in the Common Cause Education Fund and Protect Democracy models.

rows.label: One election cycle of voter information against a won voting-access reform, per dollar
rows.explainer: Outside a slide, more and better-informed voters can change who wins and what is decided, the other thing voter information changes; the site values that change for voting-access reforms through @democracy.other_reform_relative_effect (a quarter of a redistricting-movement dollar, which already holds the small partisan effect of turnout gains). This is the effect, per dollar and per year it lasts, of a cycle of registration and voter guides against a won access reform's effect per person-year of its state: a reform changes the rules for everyone in its state, while a cycle of voter information reaches the people it informs or registers (7.6 million VOTE411 users and 482,000 registrations in the year, against the tens of millions a state access reform covers), and its years are counted separately (vie_discounted_years). Candidate information may make choices better informed, but no study measures that for a voter guide. Judged a tenth (0 to 30%).

rows.label: Years one cycle of voter information shapes who governs
rows.explainer: Those elected in the cycle the work informed serve their terms: two years for the US House and most state lower houses, four for governors, senators of most states and many local offices, one for some local and primary contests. Judged 2 years (1 to 4), the House term.

rows.label: Years from the work until those elected take office
rows.explainer: The year's work led up to the November 2024 election, and those elected took office in January 2025, about half a year after the middle of the year to June 2025. Judged 0.5 years (0.25 to 1.5, the upper end for work in this year that acts on the 2026 midterms).

rows.label: Discounted years of one cycle's effect on who governs
rows.explainer: The terms served, at the shared discount rate, never more than the years a won reform counts, after the wait until they start. They replace the reform's own discounted years (maps_discounted_years) in vie_uov, so the side effect doesn't grow with $win_years_counted beyond a term.

rows.label: The Education Fund's voter-information spending over the redistricting movement's resources
rows.explainer: Its voter-information spending in the units of oth_uov (a year of reform work the size of the redistricting movement), as the other-reforms branch counts its own dollars.

rows.label: Voter-information side effects, summed
rows.explainer: The voter-information branch's side effects, each weighted by the side-effect slider. The shared backlash share (@democracy.democracy_work_backlash_share) is for litigation and campaigns seen as partisan; nonpartisan voter guides and registration don't provoke counter-measures, so it isn't read here.
